column4: BW Energy is advancing Brazil’s Maromba oil field by converting its short-term lease of the BW Maromba B Super Gorilla jack-up rig into a 10-year project lease with Minsheng Financial Leasing Co. Ltd. The arrangement finances the rig’s purchase, refurbishment, and conversion into an integrated drilling and production platform, covering approximately $274 million of previously disclosed Maromba development capital expenditure. Lease payments begin only after first oil, followed by a fixed daily rate of $120,500, reducing near-term cash requirements and improving cost predictability. After refurbishment in Dubai, the unit is expected to mobilize to Brazil for phased drilling and completion work. While no production forecast was provided, Maromba represents a future source of Brazilian crude and demonstrates how lease financing and repurposed infrastructure can support offshore production while limiting upfront capital exposure in a challenging oil-price environment.
column6: BW Energy: Signs long-term lease for the Maromba drilling and wellhead platform
column7:
BW Energy announces that the short-term lease for the Super Gorilla class jack-up rig BW MAROMBA B signed in September 2025 has been successfully converted into a long-term project lease agreement with Minsheng Financial Leasing Co. Ltd. (MSFL).
The new lease agreement covers the rig purchase and all costs required to bring the MAROMBA B wellhead platform to drilling and production readiness. This represents USD 274 million of the previously communicated Maromba CAPEX and provides an efficient lease financing structure for the project's development phase, followed by a ten-year lease term.
The lease will commence upon first oil for the Maromba development, with no payments due before this point. The lease carries a fixed daily rate of USD 120,500, providing cost predictability throughout the lease period.
"We are pleased to establish an attractive lease financing for the full scope of the Maromba wellhead platform investment, building on our strong relationship with MSFL," said Thomas Young, the CFO of BW Energy. "This agreement further highlights our ability to consistently leverage repurposed production infrastructure to enable cost-efficient greenfield developments."
The rig is currently en route from Singapore to Dubai, with expected arrival before year-end. At the yard in Dubai, it will be refurbished and converted into a fully integrated drilling and production platform. The unit's recent drilling service in Australia supports an efficient upgrade and refurbishment programme. When completed, it will mobilise to Brazil and commence drilling and completion work according to the phased development plan for the Maromba field.

column3: Sanctions Squeeze Compliant Tanker Fleet, Sending VLCC Rates Near $130,000
column4: Western sanctions on vessels carrying Iranian, Russian, and Venezuelan crude have reduced the pool of compliant tankers, while opaque ownership structures and older ships absorb much of the sanctioned trade. At the same time, OPEC and allied demand is competing for a shrinking and aging VLCC fleet, driving daily freight rates to roughly $130,000—near three-year highs. Higher shipping costs raise delivered crude prices, complicate trade routes, and can reduce effective export capacity even when oil is physically available. The tanker market is expected to remain firm through the first half of 2026, though newbuilding deliveries or weaker demand could ease rates later in the year.

column3: U.S. Seizure of M/T Skipper Escalates Crackdown, Threatening Venezuelan Oil Exports
column4: The U.S. seizure of the sanctioned VLCC M/T Skipper, formerly Adisa, after it departed Venezuela marks a significant escalation from financial sanctions to physical interdiction of Venezuelan crude. U.S. authorities, including the Coast Guard, FBI, Homeland Security and Justice Department, allege that the vessel—reportedly carrying roughly 1.1–1.9 million barrels of Venezuelan Merey and Iranian-linked crude—was part of a shadow-fleet network connected to Iran’s IRGC and Hezbollah. Washington has also sanctioned six shipping companies and signaled that additional tanker seizures may follow. The actions threaten to remove vessels and cargoes from Venezuela’s export system, delay shipments, raise insurance, compliance and retaliation risks, and deter mainstream owners, traders and buyers from handling sanctioned barrels. Venezuela’s exports, largely bound for China and Cuba, could therefore fall materially, with potential implications for heavy, sour crude availability and U.S. Gulf Coast refinery feedstocks; operational outages at Venezuela’s José complex and other facilities add to the disruption risk. Caracas has condemned the seizure as piracy, increasing the possibility of further escalation. The immediate global supply loss remains limited relative to ample inventories and broader oversupply, but the prospect of sustained enforcement has supported crude prices intermittently, widened uncertainty around Venezuelan export flows and established a geopolitical floor under Brent and WTI.
column6: Seizing Venezuelan oil tankers could backfire on Trump
column7:
Legal experts I've spoken to suggest that the oil tanker seizure, while controversial, has a stronger legal justification than the boat strikes. The tanker confiscated last week was flying a Guyana flag, but Guyana said there was no record of the ship's registration, which makes it a stateless vessel. The tanker has also been implicated in violating sanctions on both Venezuela and Iran. That could give the U.S. government the right to seize it under American law.
Capturing oil tankers is likely to do far more damage to the Maduro regime than blowing up drug boats. Maduro and his henchmen may profit from the drug trade, but the revenue being reaped by drug cartels, and hence by corrupt Venezuelan officials, is not going to be dramatically affected by the loss of a few speedboats. The seizure of oil tankers is different because Venezuela relies so heavily on oil exports.
column9: The tanker seizure has a stronger legal basis than boat strikes because the vessel was effectively stateless and allegedly violated U.S. sanctions on Venezuela and Iran; targeting oil tankers could significantly pressure Maduro by disrupting Venezuela’s vital oil-export revenues.

column6: U.S. Unseals Warrant for Tanker Seized by Coast Guard Off the Coast of Venezuela

The seizure warrant was signed by a magistrate judge of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on November 26, 2025. On December 10, the U.S. Coast Guard boarded and seized the crude oil tanker as it traveled on the high seas after departing Venezuela. The U.S. Department of the Treasurys Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) previously identified the M/T Skipper, which was formerly called the Adisa, as being used in an oil shipping network supporting Hizballah and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF), both U.S. Department of State-designated foreign terrorist organizations. The IRGC uses proceeds from the distribution of petroleum to fund its terrorist networks. As the premiere United States Attorneys office leading efforts to intercept ghost vessels as well as sanctioned products, we remain committed to legally supporting President Trumps efforts to make the world a safer place, said U.S. Attorney Pirro. The U.S. Attorneys Office in DC has demonstrated exceptional perseverance, and a unique ability to navigate the challenges inherent in this type of enforcement action unmatched anywhere in the country. The FBI's Counterintelligence Division and our partners will continue to enforce U.S. sanctions and cut off our adversaries from financial markets and critical technology, said FBI Director Patel. The seizure of this vessel highlights our successful efforts to impose costs on the governments of Venezuela and Iran.

column3: U.S. Seizure of M/T Skipper Escalates Crackdown, Threatening Venezuelan Oil Exports
column4: The U.S. seizure of the sanctioned VLCC M/T Skipper, formerly Adisa, after it departed Venezuela marks a significant escalation from financial sanctions to physical interdiction of Venezuelan crude. U.S. authorities, including the Coast Guard, FBI, Homeland Security and Justice Department, allege that the vessel—reportedly carrying roughly 1.1–1.9 million barrels of Venezuelan Merey and Iranian-linked crude—was part of a shadow-fleet network connected to Iran’s IRGC and Hezbollah. Washington has also sanctioned six shipping companies and signaled that additional tanker seizures may follow. The actions threaten to remove vessels and cargoes from Venezuela’s export system, delay shipments, raise insurance, compliance and retaliation risks, and deter mainstream owners, traders and buyers from handling sanctioned barrels. Venezuela’s exports, largely bound for China and Cuba, could therefore fall materially, with potential implications for heavy, sour crude availability and U.S. Gulf Coast refinery feedstocks; operational outages at Venezuela’s José complex and other facilities add to the disruption risk. Caracas has condemned the seizure as piracy, increasing the possibility of further escalation. The immediate global supply loss remains limited relative to ample inventories and broader oversupply, but the prospect of sustained enforcement has supported crude prices intermittently, widened uncertainty around Venezuelan export flows and established a geopolitical floor under Brent and WTI.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.

column7:
Spare capacity offers limited reassurance. Saudi Arabia and the UAE remain the only major producers able to raise output at short notice, and both are now operating closer to their expanded capacity levels. The market's vulnerability emerges if non-OPEC+ production slows, particularly in the Americas.
US shale output, resilient at around 10.6 mb/d, is beginning to show signs of levelling off. column6: Permian Basin Oil Production Peaks in December 2025, Ushering in New Era for U.S. Shale
column7:
Oil production in the Permian basin is poised to peak in December, a watershed moment for the U.S. shale boom that upended the global energy market over the past 15 years. According to a Reuters report, the Permian basin, which straddles West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, is set to produce a record-high 6.76 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil in December, only slightly higher than November's total, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said in its latest Short Term Energy Outlook.
This monthly figure may never be topped, given that most of the Permian's top-tier oil acreage has been tapped and sharply depleted after more than a decade of drilling. But improvements in drilling technology are enabling firms to explore new, often deeper formations. That means current production levels can likely be sustained for years, defying previous warnings that the shale boom would experience a precipitous decline.
This includes Exxon's $60 billion acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources in 2024 and Conoco's $22.5 billion acquisition of Marathon Oil the same year. The consolidation has helped companies innovate and cut costs, leaving them better able to withstand oil price downturns.
None more so than Exxon, which announced on Tuesday that it plans to double its Permian oil and gas output between 2024 and 2030 to 2.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd), an upgrade of 200,000 boepd compared with last year's production forecast. In a presentation on Tuesday, Exxon CEO Darren Woods said the company is using patented, lightweight proppant to improve hydraulic fractures and software to better direct drilling paths, which can extend the range of lateral wells to up to 4 miles (6.4 km).
"Put together, such innovation will drive drilling costs down by around 40% while increasing oil recovery rates in wells by 50% between 2019 and 2030," Woods said. Chevron, which plans to keep Permian production stable at 1 million bpd through 2040, is now using a technique that allows it to fracture subterranean rock in three wells simultaneously, cutting drilling time and costs. Exxon and Chevron's Permian production costs have fallen to around $30-$40 per barrel, lower than the industry average of $62.
So even though the Permian basin is unlikely to again record the stellar growth rates it enjoyed over the past decade, its production is set to plateau at a high level, meaning this region is likely to remain the bedrock of the U.S. oil industry for years to come.
FAR FROM OVER
The Permian has been the core of American shale oil since the industry took off around 2010, helping the U.S. become the world's largest oil producer as of 2018. This basin accounted for nearly half of total U.S. production of 13.6 million bpd in 2025. Permian production rose by 400,000 bpd year-on-year in December, which is particularly eye-catching because U.S. oil prices dropped below $60 a barrel this year for the first time since early 2021.
Prices at that level would have sent Permian production plummeting earlier this decade - but things have changed. Whats more, the number of active drilling rigs in the basin dropped by 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier even as production rose, according to the EIA. This highlights the industry's efficiency gains and its resilience in a lower-price environment.

column6: Imperial Oil Issues Corporate Outlook for 2026, With $2 Billion Capital Plan
column7:
05:11 PM EST, 12/15/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Imperial Oil (IMO.TO, IMO) after trade Monday issued its 2026 guidance and said it remains focused on maximizing the value of its existing assets and increasing cash flow.
Capital and exploration expenditures in 2026 are expected to be between $2 billion and $2.2 billion, the company said, adding that upstream spending will support bitumen recovery projects at it Kearl oil-sands mine, high-value infill drilling and Mahihkan SA-SAGD at Cold Lake, and mine progression at Kearl and Syncrude. Downstream investments will focus on digital upgrades and targeted projects.

column6: Stena Surprise hoists the Swedish flag
column7:
Leading tanker shipping company Stena Bulk confirms that it has reflagged its Suezmax tanker Stena Surprise under the Swedish flag, marking a significant milestone for Swedish shipping. A ceremony was held on board the vessel in Nynäshamn, Sweden. Andreas Carlson (pictured, second from right), Minister for Infrastructure and Housing, attended to witness the hoisting of the Swedish flag.
Built in 2012, Stena Surprise is the latest Suezmax tanker to join the Swedish Shipping Register, following Stena Sunrise and Stena Suede in flying the Swedish colours. The latest transfer is part of an ongoing strategic initiative to reflag some of Stena Bulk's vessels in Sweden.
Choosing to flag the vessels in Sweden highlights the strategic importance of improving the country's global shipping footprint, reinforces the nation's standing in international maritime trade, and supports a competitive and sustainable Swedish fleet.
Based on available records and internal knowledge, these Suezmax-class vessels are the first of their type to be flagged in Sweden and among only a handful of large crude carriers ever to do so.
Erik Hånell (second from left), President and CEO of Stena Bulk, said: "The reflagging of Stena Surprise is a proud moment for Stena Bulk, and it is a particular honour to have been able to do this in a Swedish port. "This initiative is a testament to the close collaboration we have with the Swedish authorities and ship registry. Welcoming this vessel under our national flag reinforces our commitment to strengthening Sweden's maritime presence."

column3: Buccaneer Energy Targets Up to 1 Million More Barrels With Pine Mills Waterflood Expansion
column4: Buccaneer Energy is expanding waterflood operations in the Fouke area of its Pine Mills field in Texas to inject water, maintain reservoir pressure, and improve recovery from mature oil assets. The field has produced 333,851 barrels through primary recovery, and the project is expected to add an estimated 667,000 to 1.002 million recoverable barrels. The planned return of the Turner #1 well before system start-up will provide interim production, underscoring the potential of secondary recovery to increase reserves and output without relying solely on new-field development.
column6: Buccaneer to boost oil production at Pine Mills field using waterflood scheme
column7:
By injecting water, Buccaneer aims to increase reservoir pressure, which is expected to stabilise and improve oil recovery rates from the field.
The company has been using waterflooding in the Pine Mills region for more than five decades. Primary recovery in the area reached 333,851 barrels (bbl) of oil as of September 2025.
Buccaneer estimates that the waterflood could yield an additional 667,000-1,002,000bbl of recoverable oil.
The Turner #1 well will return to production before the waterflood system becomes operational, providing additional output during the preparation phase, the company said.
In the Pine Mills field and surrounding areas, primary recovery typically accounts for 5-20% of the original oil in place, with an average of around 15%.
Buccaneer Energy CEO Paul Welch said: "The decision to initiate a waterflood in the Fouke area marks a key step forward in maximising long-term value from our Pine Mills assets. Waterflooding has a proven track record in these reservoirs, and we believe the Turner #1 and Daniel #1 wells provide ideal injection points to support a highly effective recovery scheme.
"We are confident that this programme will materially increase recoverable reserves and enhance the field's production profile. We look forward to updating investors as we progress the regulatory and technical workstreams required for implementation."

column6: OMS Energy Technologies Inc.'s Indonesian Subsidiary Obtains API Spec 11D1 Certification, Strengthening Industry Leadership
column7:
Expands Product Portfolio with Self-Developed Certified Components, Creating New Revenue Opportunities throughout Asia Pacific
MALAYSIA, November 27, 2025 - OMS Energy Technologies Inc. ("OMS" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: OMSE), a growth-oriented manufacturer of surface wellhead systems ("SWS") and oil country tubular goods ("OCTG") for the oil and gas industry, announced its wholly-owned subsidiary, PT OMS Oilfield Services ("OMS Indonesia"), has earned the American Petroleum Institute's API Spec 11D1 certification and expanded its product offerings with certified, self-developed and self-manufactured packers, a critical component in petroleum and natural gas operations. This milestone underscores OMS's commitment to industry-leading standards and strengthens its ability to win new business in competitive oilfield markets.
API Spec 11D1 defines design, manufacturing, testing and quality control standards for packers and bridge plugs, ensuring equipment can handle high-stress conditions and enhancing trust and confidence among operators and service companies. With the API Spec 11D1 certification, OMS Indonesia will augment its self-manufactured product portfolio of API-6A-certified surface wellheads and Christmas trees with full-scale product design, qualification, and manufacturing of retrievable mechanical and hydraulic packers. These components can be seamlessly integrated with OMS's surface wellhead systems as well as other manufacturers' equipment, offering customers flexible, high-performance solutions and creating diverse revenue opportunities.
Building on its established repair and maintenance services in Indonesia, OMS has commenced its first project integrating its certified packers with a leading Indonesian energy operator. The project is currently in the qualification stage.
Mr. How Meng Hock, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of OMS, commented, "We are proud to earn the API Spec 11D1 certification for our Indonesia operations, a significant milestone that expands our product and service capabilities in a key market. Our relentless commitment to technical excellence and innovation is paying dividends, empowering OMS to deliver a growing suite of high-performance products and solutions to a broader customer base. We will remain focused on achieving the highest possible standards for quality and safety, strengthening OMS's position as a trusted partner to leading energy producers across Asia Pacific."
The API Spec 11D1 certification not only reinforces OMS's technical leadership but also positions the company for accelerated growth in both domestic and international markets. As OMS expands its global footprint, this certification will play a pivotal role in building client confidence and securing new strategic partnerships worldwide.

column3: Global Oil Prices Face Prolonged Pressure as Supply Outpaces Weak Demand
column4: Global crude prices remain under pressure as production growth is expected to outpace relatively weak demand through 2026. Forecasts from the IEA, EIA, Barclays and other analysts point to a surplus ranging from roughly 1.9 million to 4 million barrels per day, while OPEC presents a more balanced outlook. Rising output from OPEC+, the Americas and other producers, together with weaker consumption signals from China and sluggish global industrial activity, has pushed Brent toward the low-$60s and WTI below $60, with some forecasts allowing for mid-$50 prices. Contango in the Brent curve, rising tanker inventories and crude accumulating in storage indicate that supply is exceeding near-term demand. Geopolitical disruptions and low inventories may provide temporary support, but ample alternative supply has limited their price impact. Prolonged weakness could prompt producers to cut output, defer investment and reduce capacity, helping the market rebalance from 2027 onward, while OPEC+ retains the ability to respond if conditions deteriorate.
column6: Oil markets sink as Brent slips under $60 and WTI hits $55
column7:
Brent broke below $60 and sent a shock across the oil market, dropping to $59.96 after a steady grind lower through 2025. WTI followed the move and sat near $55.
Traders watched the decline build for months as supply kept rising while demand stayed weak.
The market has been flooded by fresh barrels from OPEC+ and producers across the Americas, and forecasts show that imbalance getting even worse next year. The year's loss deepened fast, and no one seemed surprised anymore.
The shift in mood also came from renewed hope that Russia's war in Ukraine could move toward a settlement. That hope cut into the geopolitical premium that had held crude higher for years.
At the same time, investors tried to measure the impact of U.S. pressure on Venezuela. With President Trump still pushing hard on sanctions strategy, traders kept guessing how Venezuelan flows might shift.

column7:

Paul, West Texas Intermediate crude - what's driving it lower, and do you see that changing?
PAUL: I think a lot of it comes down to overcapacity. We've seen excess supply build up in the oil business, with OPEC increasing capacity and then keeping production at elevated levels. At the same time, there's been significant output from U.S. shale producers. All of that has contributed to the oversupply we're seeing, and I don't think that gets worked through over the next couple of months at least.
Canadian investors are reassessing energy exposure and resource dealmaking as oil prices slide sharply and Ottawa moves quickly on a major mining acquisition.
BNN Bloomberg spoke with Paul Harris, portfolio manager at Harris Douglas Asset Management, about the impact of oversupply on crude prices, the approval of the Teck-Anglo deal and which sectors he believes are best positioned heading into 2026.
Key Takeaways
Excess oil supply from OPEC and U.S. shale production is pressuring crude prices, with little relief expected in the near term.
Large-cap Canadian oil producers are better positioned to weather lower prices due to strong balance sheets, steady dividends and acquisition capacity.
Ottawa's rapid approval of the Teck-Anglo deal surprised investors, with execution and follow-through on Canadian commitments now the key risk.
Mining consolidation makes strategic sense given the importance of critical minerals like copper, though synergies are limited in the sector.
Financials, technology and health care remain preferred sectors, supported by low interest rates, regulatory changes and consolidation opportunities.

Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude contract dipped 0.7% to $56.44 a barrel, while Murban futures declined 0.7% at $61.17/bbl. Both contracts were seen hovering near their lowest since early May.
"Crude oil fell as the market weighed up signs of optimism on a peace deal being reached between Russia and Ukraine," ANZ analysts said.
On Monday, European negotiators reported that the peace talks are making progress.
"During the meeting we discussed Security Guarantees for Ukrain... At the conclusion of the meetings, I called President Putin, and began the arrangements for a meeting, at a location to be determined, between President Putin and President Zelenskyy," US President Donald trump said in a post on X.
"This raised concerns that recent US sanctions on Russian oil companies would be ultimately lifted, adding to an already well supplied market," ANZ analysts added.
The oil market is now awaiting crucial inventory data from the Energy Information Administration.
Meanwhile, weekly US crude inventory data from the EIA is expected to show a 2.2-million-barrel build for the week ending Dec.12, Macquarie strategists said in a weekly note on Monday.

column6: Middle East Oil Market Weakens as Glut Concerns Gain Traction
column7:
Within the region, differentials between some spot crudes and the Dubai benchmark have softened, according to the General Index. Upper Zakum and Oman had a 50- to 60-cent (RM2.04- to RM2.45) premium to Dubai at the end of last week, down from about 90 cents at the start of the month.
On a global basis, ING forecasts supply will rise 2.1 million barrels a day next year while demand expands about 800,000 barrels. The IEA, meanwhile, projects output will exceed consumption by 3.8 million barrels a day in 2026.
"The scale of the surplus and the expected build in inventory should put the forward curve under additional pressure," said Patterson, referring to the pricing of crude over the coming months.
Uploaded by Arion Yeow
Reflecting the abundant availability of near-term supplies, state producer Saudi Aramco recently cut the price of its flagship crude grade for Asia to the lowest level in five years. In addition, the Paris-based International Energy Agency forecasts that there will be a record global crude glut next year.
"The surplus in the oil market is set to grow in 2026, following Opec+'s decision to unwind supply cuts at a quicker-than-expected pace," said Warren Patterson, head of commodities strategy at ING Groep NV. "Non-pec supply is also expected to grow at a healthy clip despite this year's price weakness."
Other markers in the Middle East are also flashing weakness. Among them, the Dubai benchmark's discount to Brent, known as the Brent-Dubai EFS, was recently at its widest in about seven weeks.

column6: Wall Street slips as oil prices keep dropping
column7:
On Wall Street, the sharpest losses came from companies in the oil business as prices for crude kept sliding.
Expectations that companies are pumping more than enough oil to meet the world's demand have sent the price for a barrel of benchmark U.S. crude to its lowest level since 2021. It fell 2.7% Monday, as did Brent crude, the international standard. U.S. crude settled at $55.27 per barrel, while Brent settled at $58.92.
That drove APA's stock down 5.2%. Marathon Petroleum sank 4.7% and Halliburton dropped 4.3% for some of Wall Street's larger losses.
Artificial-intelligence technology stocks, meanwhile, were mixed after dominating the market in recent days.
Oracle rose 2%, and Broadcom added 0.4%. They both had dropped to sharp losses last week , even though both reported stronger profits for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

column3: Russia-Ukraine Peace Hopes Send Oil Below $60 as Traders Price In Sanctions Relief
column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.
column6: Crude Oil Prices Fall Amid Optimism About Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
column7:
05:31 AM EST, 12/16/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Crude oil prices dropped on Tuesday amid positive developments in the Russia-Ukraine peace talks, as a deal would release additional Russian oil into the market and exacerbate any surplus.
Brent crude at last look fell 1.7% to US$59.52/barrel and West Texas Intermediate crude declined 1.9% to $55.77/b. Both benchmarks are approaching their lowest levels since May, Reuters said in a Tuesday report.
This comes as the U.S. offered to provide NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine and European negotiators on Monday reported progress to end the war, the report said.
"Brent has dropped this morning to below $60 per barrel for the first time in months, as the market assesses a potential peace deal resulting in additional Russian volumes becoming available and oversupplying the market further," Reuters quoted Rystad analyst Janiv Shah as saying.
Weak Chinese economic data released Monday, including a slowdown in factory output growth and disappointing retail sales growth, also sparked concerns that global demand may not be strong enough to absorb supply growth, IG market analyst Tony Sycamore said, as quoted by Reuters.
Brent crude at last look fell 1.7% to US$59.52/barrel and West Texas Intermediate crude declined 1.9% to $55.77/b. Both benchmarks are approaching their lowest levels since May, Reuters said in a Tuesday report.

column4: Weaker-than-expected Chinese factory output and retail sales are raising concerns about crude demand in the world’s largest oil importer, particularly as global supply expands. column6: Murban Crude Premium Hits Two-Week Low on Rising Supply
column7:
According to a Reuters report, the spot premium for the Middle East crude benchmark Murban fell to its lowest level in two weeks on Monday, pressured by ample supply of the grade and rising production in the region.
Meanwhile, news that Kazakhstan hopes to bring forward moorings delivery to the CPC's Black Sea oil terminal lifted the overall oil supply outlook. Kazakhstans Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said the delivery of two new mooring points to the Caspian Pipeline Consortiums terminal has been brought forward to January from April. Premiums for Oman and Dubai were little changed on Monday, with cash Dubai's premium to swaps rising 1 cent to 55 cents a barrel.
In deal activity, Equinor will deliver two February Upper Zakum crude cargoes to Glencore following the deals. In other news, China's crude oil throughput rose 3.9% in November, as a new batch of crude oil import quotas for independent refiners offset maintenance at some state-owned refineries.
column9: Ample Middle Eastern supply, rising regional output and potentially faster Kazakh export capacity weakened Murban premiums and reinforced global oversupply concerns, while China’s 3.9% November refinery-throughput growth—driven by new independent-refiner import quotas—did little to ease broader worries about oil-demand strength.

column4: Macquarie Group expects the EIA to report a 2.2-million-barrel U.S. crude inventory build for the week ending December 12, reversing the prior week’s 1.8-million-barrel draw. The increase is attributed to slightly lower refinery runs, marginally higher imports, reduced exports, and a 400,000-barrel-per-day rise in domestic supply; the Strategic Petroleum Reserve could add about 300,000 barrels. column6: EMEA Oil Update: Prices hit 7-month low as Russia-Ukraine Peace Hopes Ease Supply Concerns
column7:
03:05 AM EST, 12/16/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Crude futures dipped to its lowest levels in more than seven months on Tuesday pressured by renewed optimism over a Russia-Ukraine peace deal as traders anticipated the return of Russian barrels to a market already struggling with supply glut fears.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude contract dipped 0.7% to $56.44 a barrel, while Murban futures declined 0.7% at $61.17/bbl. Both contracts were seen hovering near their lowest since early May.
"Crude oil fell as the market weighed up signs of optimism on a peace deal being reached between Russia and Ukraine," ANZ analysts said.
On Monday, European negotiators reported that the peace talks are making progress.
"During the meeting we discussed Security Guarantees for Ukrain... At the conclusion of the meetings, I called President Putin, and began the arrangements for a meeting, at a location to be determined, between President Putin and President Zelenskyy," US President Donald trump said in a post on X.
"This raised concerns that recent US sanctions on Russian oil companies would be ultimately lifted, adding to an already well supplied market," ANZ analysts added.
The oil market is now awaiting crucial inventory data from the Energy Information Administration.
Meanwhile, weekly US crude inventory data from the EIA is expected to show a 2.2-million-barrel build for the week ending Dec.12, Macquarie strategists said in a weekly note on Monday.

column3: Global Oil Prices Face Prolonged Pressure as Supply Outpaces Weak Demand
column4: Global crude prices remain under pressure as production growth is expected to outpace relatively weak demand through 2026. Forecasts from the IEA, EIA, Barclays and other analysts point to a surplus ranging from roughly 1.9 million to 4 million barrels per day, while OPEC presents a more balanced outlook. Rising output from OPEC+, the Americas and other producers, together with weaker consumption signals from China and sluggish global industrial activity, has pushed Brent toward the low-$60s and WTI below $60, with some forecasts allowing for mid-$50 prices. column7:
Within the region, differentials between some spot crudes and the Dubai benchmark have softened, according to the General Index. Upper Zakum and Oman had a 50- to 60-cent (RM2.04- to RM2.45) premium to Dubai at the end of last week, down from about 90 cents at the start of the month.
On a global basis, ING forecasts supply will rise 2.1 million barrels a day next year while demand expands about 800,000 barrels. The IEA, meanwhile, projects output will exceed consumption by 3.8 million barrels a day in 2026.
"The scale of the surplus and the expected build in inventory should put the forward curve under additional pressure," said Patterson, referring to the pricing of crude over the coming months.
Uploaded by Arion Yeow
Reflecting the abundant availability of near-term supplies, state producer Saudi Aramco recently cut the price of its flagship crude grade for Asia to the lowest level in five years. In addition, the Paris-based International Energy Agency forecasts that there will be a record global crude glut next year.
"The surplus in the oil market is set to grow in 2026, following Opec+'s decision to unwind supply cuts at a quicker-than-expected pace," said Warren Patterson, head of commodities strategy at ING Groep NV. "Non-pec supply is also expected to grow at a healthy clip despite this year's price weakness."
Other markers in the Middle East are also flashing weakness. Among them, the Dubai benchmark's discount to Brent, known as the Brent-Dubai EFS, was recently at its widest in about seven weeks.

column3: Weak Refinery Margins Curb Crude Buying, Swell Floating Storage and Pressure Oil Prices
column4: Weakening refinery economics are reducing near-term crude purchasing. Crude crack spreads have fallen to multi-month lows, cutting refiners’ incentive to process additional barrels into gasoline and distillates. The resulting demand weakness is evident in Saudi Aramco’s January cut to the Asian Arab Light selling price—the lowest since January 2021—and in Vortexa’s 5.1% week-over-week increase in crude held on tankers for at least seven days, to 120.23 million barrels. This floating-storage build suggests excess supply is being deferred rather than absorbed, loosening the market balance and pressuring WTI, Brent, and the forward curve. Refinery activity is uneven: stronger US throughput and improved Mexican reliability offer support, while delays in India, Iran, and Angola, maintenance at Kuwait’s al Zour refinery, and lower expected Chinese runs weigh on demand. Product imbalances are adding to the pressure, as earlier strong distillate margins encouraged diesel-heavy runs that also produced excess gasoline, pushing RBOB futures into contango. Although tight product markets and sanctions-related disruptions could improve margins in 2026, weak cracks, maintenance, and uneven utilization currently discourage incremental crude buying and reinforce bearish price pressure.

column3: Weak Refinery Margins Curb Crude Buying, Swell Floating Storage and Pressure Oil Prices
column4: Weakening refinery economics are reducing near-term crude purchasing. Crude crack spreads have fallen to multi-month lows, cutting refiners’ incentive to process additional barrels into gasoline and distillates. The resulting demand weakness is evident in Saudi Aramco’s January cut to the Asian Arab Light selling price—the lowest since January 2021—and in Vortexa’s 5.1% week-over-week increase in crude held on tankers for at least seven days, to 120.23 million barrels. This floating-storage build suggests excess supply is being deferred rather than absorbed, loosening the market balance and pressuring WTI, Brent, and the forward curve. Refinery activity is uneven: stronger US throughput and improved Mexican reliability offer support, while delays in India, Iran, and Angola, maintenance at Kuwait’s al Zour refinery, and lower expected Chinese runs weigh on demand. Product imbalances are adding to the pressure, as earlier strong distillate margins encouraged diesel-heavy runs that also produced excess gasoline, pushing RBOB futures into contango. Although tight product markets and sanctions-related disruptions could improve margins in 2026, weak cracks, maintenance, and uneven utilization currently discourage incremental crude buying and reinforce bearish price pressure.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.

Electric hydraulic fracking uses electric motors to drive hydraulic pumps, rather than diesel engines. The EIA spokesperson explains that this "leads to higher efficiency at the expense of some upfront cost".
Electric pumps improve efficiency because they lose less energy to heat and friction and convert a higher percentage of input energy into useful work; they also offer the advantage of reduced emissions and noise.

column3: 78% Tax and Falling Output Drive UK North Sea Consolidation
column4: The UK North Sea is undergoing rapid consolidation as declining production, limited new-field approvals and a 78% marginal tax rate constrain organic investment. Output fell from about 1.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2020 to roughly 474,000 boe/d by September 2025, while no new field approvals were granted for two consecutive years. Against this backdrop, TotalEnergies, Repsol UK and HitecVision plan to combine their exploration and production assets in NEO NEXT+, creating the UK’s largest independent oil and gas producer, with TotalEnergies holding 47.5%, HitecVision 28.88% and Repsol UK 23.63%. The portfolio includes Elgin/Franklin, Penguins, Mariner, Shearwater, Culzean, Alwyn North and Dunbar, and is expected to produce more than 250,000 boe/d in 2026. Deals involving Harbour Energy, TotalEnergies, Shell, Equinor, Ithaca Energy and Serica Energy—including Serica’s £57 million purchase of Spirit Energy’s southern North Sea assets—are concentrating more than 500,000 boe/d among fewer operators, as companies pursue scale, efficiency and resilience in a mature basin under growing fiscal pressure.
column6: UK North Sea Oil Merges Its Way Through Decline
column7: The UK North Sea is being reshaped by consolidation at a pace not seen since the aftermath of the 2014 oil price crash. In the past twelve months alone, a series of mergers has concentrated more than 500,000 boe/d of production into a handful of operators, as companies respond to a 78% marginal tax rate, falling output and an investment environment that has effectively closed to new developments. Deals involving Harbour Energy, TotalEnergies, Shell, Equinor and Ithaca Energy have created fewer but larger players managing a basin where production has fallen from 1.1 million b/d in 2020 to about 474,000 b/d by September 2025, and where no new field approvals have been granted for two consecutive years.

Brent broke below $60 and sent a shock across the oil market, dropping to $59.96 after a steady grind lower through 2025. WTI followed the move and sat near $55.
Traders watched the decline build for months as supply kept rising while demand stayed weak.
The market has been flooded by fresh barrels from OPEC+ and producers across the Americas, and forecasts show that imbalance getting even worse next year. The year's loss deepened fast, and no one seemed surprised anymore.
The shift in mood also came from renewed hope that Russia's war in Ukraine could move toward a settlement. That hope cut into the geopolitical premium that had held crude higher for years.
At the same time, investors tried to measure the impact of U.S. pressure on Venezuela. With President Trump still pushing hard on sanctions strategy, traders kept guessing how Venezuelan flows might shift.

column3: Russia-Ukraine Peace Hopes Send Oil Below $60 as Traders Price In Sanctions Relief
column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.
column6: Oil settles near five-year low amid ample supply, Russia-Ukraine progress
column7:
The six-month Brent futures spread moved into a contango for the first time since October.
Barclays analysts expect Brent to average US$65/bbl in 2026, slightly ahead of the forward curve, due to the expected 1.9 million bpd surplus they see as being priced in already.
"This price decline underscores the structural dynamics of today's energy market-ample supply and sluggish demand. Unless geopolitical risks or policy shifts intervene, this softness could persist well into next year," KPMG US Energy Strategy Leader Angie Gildea wrote in a note.
Adding to the pressure, soft Chinese economic data on Monday further fuelled concerns that global demand may not be strong enough to absorb recent supply growth, said IG market analyst Tony Sycamore.
China's factory output growth slowed to a 15-month low, official data showed. Retail sales also grew at their slowest pace since December 2022, during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Fears of an oversupply were marginally offset by the US seizing an oil tanker off Venezuela last week, but traders and analysts said a glut of floating storage and a surge in Chinese buying from Venezuela in anticipation of sanctions were also limiting the market impact.

column3: China’s Oil Stockpiling Cushions Crude Market as Imports Outpace Consumption by 1.9 Million Barrels a Day
column4: China has become a major temporary stabilizer for the crude market through rapid stockpiling into strategic and commercial reserves. OilX estimates Chinese storage caverns are only about half full, leaving substantial capacity for further purchases. In November, China imported more crude than it processed or consumed by roughly 1.9 million barrels per day, while reserve accumulation averaged about 1 million barrels per day during the first 11 months and imports reached a more-than-two-year high. This buying absorbed much of the global oversupply and provided intermittent price support, potentially continuing into 2026. However, the outlook depends on Beijing sustaining inventory growth rather than strong underlying demand, as weak factory output and retail sales raise doubts about the pace of future stockpiling, despite the IEA’s upward revision to oil-demand forecasts.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column3: US Shale Productivity Surge Keeps Output Rising Despite Fewer Rigs
column4: US shale supply is increasingly shaped by drilling economics, productivity gains, and expanding service capacity. The EIA raised its 2025 US crude-production forecast to 13.59 million barrels per day, helping shift expectations from a market deficit toward surplus. Producers are sustaining or increasing output with fewer rigs: Texas oil and gas production rose 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% decline in operating rigs, while rig productivity improved 14.1% year over year in the Permian and 8.7% in the Eagle Ford. Nonetheless, lower prices are driving greater selectivity, with US rigs down 6.96% year over year to 548 and Permian rigs down 18.09% to 249 as of December 12. Technology and improved recovery efforts by companies including Chevron and ExxonMobil could extend production strength, although Wood Mackenzie expects Lower 48 output eventually to decline after plateauing in the early 2030s. Service-sector investment is also supporting efficiency: Total Sand Solutions’ acquisition of Sand Revolution expands logistics coverage in the Permian and Eagle Ford, while Iron Oak Energy’s acquisition of Superior Silica Sands adds more than three million tons per year of Eagle Ford capacity and raises total production capability to about 40 million tons. Together, these productivity improvements and stronger frac-sand infrastructure may prolong US shale’s role as a key source of incremental non-OPEC supply even as drilling activity moderates.

column6: Total Sand Solutions of Fort Worth acquires Midland's Sand Revolution
column7:
Fort Worth-based Total Sand Solutions recently acquired Midland's Sand Revolution, which provides trucking, logistics and delivery solutions in Permian Basin in west Texas and Eagle Ford Shale in south Texas. Total Sand said it now becomes "the largest independent logistics provider in the country with the capacity to deliver over 25 million tons of proppant per year to its customers."
The transaction expands Total Sand's market share and geographic coverage in Permian and Eagle Ford, which account for more than half of U.S. total proppant demand.
Stuart Weinman, CEO of Total Sand Solutions, said Nov. 6, "Sand Revolution's last-mile solutions are highly complementary to our existing capabilities, allowing us to deliver even greater value, reliability and efficiency to our customers." Greg Lanham, CEO of Sand Revolution, added, "We are proud of what we've built, and joining TSS is an exciting new chapter for Sand Revolution."
The post appeared first on Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine .

column6: Crude Slips Below $60 on Ukraine Peace Talks, Possible Return of Russian Supply, Rystad Says
column7:
02:50 PM EST, 12/16/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Crude fell below $60 a barrel for the first time since February 2021 as optimism of a possible Ukraine peace deal, fueling expectations that Russian crude could re-enter global markets, Rystad Energy strategists said in a note on Tuesday.
"In the event of a ceasefire, US sanctions on Russian oil companies would likely be lifted relatively quickly, while European sanctions would probably be removed more gradually. At the same time, attacks on Russian oil infrastructure would come to an end," Jorge Leon, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy.
European gas prices slid in tandem, reinforcing a broader pullback across energy markets.
Brent futures dipped below the $60 threshold, while benchmark European gas prices fell below 27 euros a megawatt-hour, about 16% lower than in mid-November, as traders reassessed geopolitical risk premiums.

column6: Buccaneer Energy targets higher output at Pine Mills through new waterflood unit
column7:
Buccaneer Energy has outlined the next phase of development at its Fouke area assets in the Pine Mills field, Texas, moving forward with a secondary recovery program following a technical review of recent drilling and newly acquired offset acreage.
The company plans to implement a waterflood scheme using the Turner #1 and Daniel #1 wells as injection wells. Located at the downdip limits of the productive reservoir, both wells are considered optimal for establishing pressure support and improving long-term recovery. Buccaneer holds a 32.5% working interest in the area.
Waterflooding has been used in the Pine Mills region for more than five decades, typically increasing recovery factors from about 15% under primary production to between 30% and 50%. Current estimates suggest the Fouke waterflood project could unlock between 667,000 and 1,002,000 additional barrels of oil, compared with 333,851 barrels recovered to date under primary production.
Before operations can begin, Buccaneer must secure approval from the Texas Railroad Commission to form a waterflood unit that includes all leaseholders and royalty owners. Establishing the unit and constructing associated facilities is expected to take up to six months.
During this preparation period, the Turner #1 well will be returned to production, adding incremental output while regulatory and engineering work progresses. Once the waterflood is online, Buccaneer plans to drill the Fouke #4 well and sidetrack the Allar #1 well.
CEO Paul Welch said the decision represents a significant step toward maximizing long-term value from Pine Mills. "Waterflooding has a proven track record in these reservoirs, and we believe the Turner #1 and Daniel #1 wells provide ideal injection points to support a highly effective recovery scheme," he said.
Further updates will be issued as development advances.

column6: Baker Hughes strikes framework deal with Hunt Oil on mature fields
column7:
(Alliance News) - Baker Hughes Co on Monday announced a joint framework deal with Dallas,Texas-based Hunt Oil Co to evaluate and redevelop mature oil and gas fields worldwide.
The Houston, Texas-based oilfield services firm said it will combine its subsurface insights, mature asset solutions and technology expertise with Hunt Oil's global upstream exploration and operations experience.
Together, the companies aim to identify and assess opportunities to extend the productive life of some of the world's most prolific basins.
Baker Hughes said the collaboration will support redevelopment strategies and optimise recovery from existing fields.
Baker Hughes Chief Executive Officer Lorenzo Simonell said: "We welcome this collaboration with Hunt Oil as a meaningful step toward unlocking new value from mature fields. Strategic collaborations like this exemplify how we can scale progress and deliver impactful solutions for the energy sector globally."
Hunt Oil CEO Hunter Hunt added: "We are thrilled to combine Hunt's entrepreneurial approach to energy development with Baker Hughes' extensive product offerings and technical expertise to resuscitate oil and gas fields that could become material producers of hydrocarbons if they had the right investment."
Shares in Baker Hughes closed up 0.1% at USD46.89 in New York on Monday.

column3: 78% Tax and Falling Output Drive UK North Sea Consolidation
column4: The UK North Sea is undergoing rapid consolidation as declining production, limited new-field approvals and a 78% marginal tax rate constrain organic investment. Output fell from about 1.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2020 to roughly 474,000 boe/d by September 2025, while no new field approvals were granted for two consecutive years. Against this backdrop, TotalEnergies, Repsol UK and HitecVision plan to combine their exploration and production assets in NEO NEXT+, creating the UK’s largest independent oil and gas producer, with TotalEnergies holding 47.5%, HitecVision 28.88% and Repsol UK 23.63%. The portfolio includes Elgin/Franklin, Penguins, Mariner, Shearwater, Culzean, Alwyn North and Dunbar, and is expected to produce more than 250,000 boe/d in 2026. Deals involving Harbour Energy, TotalEnergies, Shell, Equinor, Ithaca Energy and Serica Energy—including Serica’s £57 million purchase of Spirit Energy’s southern North Sea assets—are concentrating more than 500,000 boe/d among fewer operators, as companies pursue scale, efficiency and resilience in a mature basin under growing fiscal pressure.
column6: PDMR Dealings
column7:
Notes to Editors
Serica Energy is an independent British oil and gas company with a broad portfolio of assets located in the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS). The Company is responsible for about 5% of the UK's natural gas, which plays a significant role in supporting the country's energy transition, and has invested over £1 billion in the UK supply chain since 2020. Serica maintains a balanced output of oil and gas across its operations.
The Company's key producing assets are grouped around two major hubs: the Bruce, Keith, and Rhum fields in the Northern North Sea, where Serica is the operator; and a mix of operated and non-operated fields connected to the Triton FPSO in the Central North Sea.
Serica aims to create shareholder value through a mix of production from existing oil and gas fields, organic investment and M&A.
Serica expects to complete the purchase of Prax Upstream Limited during 2025, gaining 100% ownership and operatorship of the Lancaster field situated in the West of Shetlands area. In H1 2026, Serica is also set to complete the acquisition of a 40% operated stake in the Greater Laggan Area offshore fields and associated Shetland Gas Plant from TotalEnergies and non-operated interests in the Catcher and Golden Eagle Area Development fields from ONE-Dyas.
Serica's shares trade on the AIM market of the London Stock Exchange (ticker: SQZ).

column3: Global Oil Prices Face Prolonged Pressure as Supply Outpaces Weak Demand
column4: Global crude prices remain under pressure as production growth is expected to outpace relatively weak demand through 2026. Forecasts from the IEA, EIA, Barclays and other analysts point to a surplus ranging from roughly 1.9 million to 4 million barrels per day, while OPEC presents a more balanced outlook. Rising output from OPEC+, the Americas and other producers, together with weaker consumption signals from China and sluggish global industrial activity, has pushed Brent toward the low-$60s and WTI below $60, with some forecasts allowing for mid-$50 prices. Contango in the Brent curve, rising tanker inventories and crude accumulating in storage indicate that supply is exceeding near-term demand. Geopolitical disruptions and low inventories may provide temporary support, but ample alternative supply has limited their price impact. Prolonged weakness could prompt producers to cut output, defer investment and reduce capacity, helping the market rebalance from 2027 onward, while OPEC+ retains the ability to respond if conditions deteriorate.

Superior Silica Sands is a Texas-based mining company and a leading provider of proppant to the Eagle Ford Shale, as well as high-quality sand solutions for the industrial, construction, and sports sectors across South Texas and the surrounding region. The company's San Antonio mining facility includes two distinct, state-of-the-art plants: the Frac Sand plant and the Industrials plant. Superior Silica Sands is headquartered in San Antonio, Texas.
With the Superior Silica acquisition, Iron Oak Energy's total annual production capacity increases to ~40 million tons, serving both oil and natural gas basins. In addition to its Eagle Ford Shale assets, Iron Oak Energy operates five large-scale facilities in the Permian Basin and three premier Northern White sand facilities.

Iron Oak Energy is a leading diversified proppant provider in North America with eleven active production facilities and the capability to supply every major shale basin across North America. column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.

column3: Lower Oil Prices Trigger U.S. Shale Retreat, Threatening Future Supply
column4: Lower crude prices are reducing U.S. drilling and discouraging new shale investment. Baker Hughes reported declines in active rigs in the Permian Basin and nationwide, with the U.S. count well below year-earlier levels, signaling tighter capital spending and slower future production growth as WTI and regional prices weaken. Sustained Brent and WTI prices in the mid-$50s to low-$60s could make some hydraulic-fracturing projects uneconomic, although longer laterals, electric fracking and AI-assisted targeting are allowing the most efficient producers to remain profitable at lower prices. Bank of America estimates that WTI averaging $57 per barrel in 2026 could reduce U.S. shale output by about 70,000 barrels per day, or 1%, while Bracewell sees Brent near $55 as insufficient for aggressive expansion. Persistently weak prices may eventually curb supply, helping stabilize prices near $70, but Saudi Arabia’s support for lower prices could prolong near-term weakness and increase its fiscal pressures. Goldman Sachs expects a possible mid-2026 low followed by recovery as demand rises, Russian supply declines and non-OPEC growth slows, meaning today’s price-driven investment cuts could ultimately help create a market deficit.
column6: A year on from 'drill, baby, drill', why are there fewer oil rigs in the US?
column7:
The declining rig count and inclining productivity is explained by efficiency improvements. This includes the drilling of longer laterals in the most productive plays, such as the Permian.
The American Petroleum Institute reports that, in 2025, the average length of laterals in the Midland Basin in the Permian region were 58% longer than in 2015, while Rystad notes that over 50% of wells completed in 2025 have spanned more than 10,500ft (two miles) laterally, with the longest reaching 21,276 ft (four miles). Improvements in drilling technology have driven these figures, including horizontal drilling and electric hydraulic fracturing.
Electric hydraulic fracking uses electric motors to drive hydraulic pumps, rather than diesel engines. The EIA spokesperson explains that this "leads to higher efficiency at the expense of some upfront cost".
column9: Despite declining rig counts, U.S. shale productivity is rising through efficiency gains, particularly longer horizontal wells and electric hydraulic fracturing in the Permian. These technologies boost near-term output and reduce operating inefficiencies, but higher upfront costs may constrain investment under low oil prices, potentially masking a retreat that threatens future supply growth.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.
column6: A year on from 'drill, baby, drill', why are there fewer oil rigs in the US?
column7:
The declining rig count and inclining productivity is explained by efficiency improvements. This includes the drilling of longer laterals in the most productive plays, such as the Permian.
The American Petroleum Institute reports that, in 2025, the average length of laterals in the Midland Basin in the Permian region were 58% longer than in 2015, while Rystad notes that over 50% of wells completed in 2025 have spanned more than 10,500ft (two miles) laterally, with the longest reaching 21,276 ft (four miles). Improvements in drilling technology have driven these figures, including horizontal drilling and electric hydraulic fracturing.
Electric hydraulic fracking uses electric motors to drive hydraulic pumps, rather than diesel engines. The EIA spokesperson explains that this "leads to higher efficiency at the expense of some upfront cost".
column9: Despite declining rig counts, U.S. shale productivity is rising through efficiency gains, particularly longer horizontal wells and electric hydraulic fracturing in the Permian. These technologies boost near-term output and reduce operating inefficiencies, but higher upfront costs may constrain investment under low oil prices, potentially masking a retreat that threatens future supply growth.

column3: Fracture Design and Reservoir Stress Hold the Key to Boosting Tight-Oil Recovery
column4: Tight-oil recovery depends strongly on how hydraulic-fracturing design interacts with reservoir stress and geological structure. Experimental and numerical studies in deep tight sandstone show that lower geostress differences promote complex, branched fracture networks, while higher stress differences constrain lateral growth and align fractures with the maximum horizontal stress. Injection volume, fluid viscosity, bedding planes, and the strength of natural weak surfaces also control fracture complexity: lower volumes reduce early bifurcation, whereas low-viscosity fluids can encourage branching. Optimizing these parameters increases stimulated reservoir volume and contacted oil-bearing rock, improving unconventional crude-oil recovery. The commercial importance of such completion strategies is reflected by service and equipment providers such as NCS Multistage and Kobold, which support multistage horizontal-well fracturing.

Hydraulic Fracturing Test Equipment and Process
The high- and low-temperature multiphase flow fracturing physics simulation test system (as shown in Figure 2), composed of a stress loading system, heating temperature control system, water pressure injection system, integrated control system, and monitoring and testing system, can realize deep high-temperature true three-axis hydraulic fracturing tests.A servo loading system is used to apply constant true triaxial stress to the specimen to simulate the stress state of deep formation. The servo pump pressure control system is equipped with a program controller, which can maintain a constant flow rate or follow a preset injection program. During the test process, the data acquisition system is used to record the pump pressure, displacement, and other parameters. An AE monitoring system is used to monitor the AE signal inside the specimen during fracturing to determine the rupture time point and location of the specimen. The experimental procedure is as follows:(1) Sample preparation and installation: Place the prepared rock sample in the center of the true triaxial loading frame. Install the fracturing fluid injection pipeline at the predetermined location of the rock sample and ensure its sealed connection with the subsequent water pressure injection system. (2) Stress loading and temperature control: Activate the servo loading system and apply constant and independent triaxial stress to the rock sample through six loading plates to simulate the true stress state of deep formations. Activate the heating and temperature control system to heat the rock sample and surrounding environment to the target temperature.
Studying the propagation behavior of hydraulic fracturing fractures is of great significance for understanding the mechanism of fracture propagation in deep unconventional reservoirs. The goal of unconventional oil and gas reservoir fracturing transformation is to form a complex fracture network system and increase the effective transformation volume of the reservoir. This article conducts physical model experiments on fracturing under different reservoir stress conditions to determine whether complex pressure fractures can be formed. The main controlling factors for the formation of complex pressure fractures are analyzed, and the influence of each factor is quantitatively studied through numerical simulation. The results indicate that the difference in geostress has a significant impact on the formation of pressure cracks. As the difference in geostress increases, the lateral extension range of pressure cracks significantly decreases, resulting in a phenomenon parallel to the direction of maximum horizontal geostress. As the injection volume decreases, the phenomenon of early fracturing bifurcation propagation gradually decreases, with a small number of bifurcations appearing. In the subsequent fracturing process, the main trend of fracture extension is more pronounced in reservoirs with lower fluid injection rates. In addition, low-viscosity fracturing fluids seem to be more prone to forming fracture zones with more developed branching fractures. This study can provide technical support and reference for fracturing construction in deep tight oil reservoirs.

column7:
A recent ruling by the Federal Court of Appeal in NCS Multistage Inc. v. Kobold Corporation provides critical clarification on three key aspects of Canadian patent law: claim construction, obviousness-type double patenting, and the proper approach to awarding lump-sum costs. This decision offers important guidance on interpreting claim scope, assessing patentable distinctiveness under the first-to-file regime, and ensuring procedural fairness in cost awards.
Background and trial decision
The parties to the proceeding, NCS and Kobold, are competitors that supply services and equipment for hydraulic fracking in the oil and gas industry.
At trial, the issues included: NCS's allegations of infringement by Kobold of six of NCS's patents; Kobold's counterclaim alleging the invalidity of NCS's patents; and Kobold's counterclaim that NCS infringed Kobold's 571 Patent. The patents at issue involved tools and sleeves used to drill multistage horizontal oil wells for hydrocarbons.

column4: Lower crude prices are reducing U.S. drilling and discouraging new shale investment. column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.
