Baker Hughes reported declines in active rigs in the Permian Basin and nationwide, with the U.S. count well below year-earlier levels, signaling tighter capital spending and slower future production growth as WTI and regional prices weaken. Sustained Brent and WTI prices in the mid-$50s to low-$60s could make some hydraulic-fracturing projects uneconomic, although longer laterals, electric fracking and AI-assisted targeting are allowing the most efficient producers to remain profitable at lower prices. Bank of America estimates that WTI averaging $57 per barrel in 2026 could reduce U.S. shale output by about 70,000 barrels per day, or 1%, while Bracewell sees Brent near $55 as insufficient for aggressive expansion. Persistently weak prices may eventually curb supply, helping stabilize prices near $70, but Saudi Arabia’s support for lower prices could prolong near-term weakness and increase its fiscal pressures. Goldman Sachs expects a possible mid-2026 low followed by recovery as demand rises, Russian supply declines and non-OPEC growth slows, meaning today’s price-driven investment cuts could ultimately help create a market deficit.

"Even though prices have fallen, refueling is still relatively expensive," says ADAC fuel market expert Christian Laberer. "And the current recovery can quickly turn around again if there are international crises - especially in the Middle East." This is because by far the most important factor for the development of fuel prices is the crude oil price.
Looking ahead is difficult
Accordingly, looking ahead is difficult. In fact, only a small increase around the turn of the year is somewhat foreseeable. The upcoming increase in the CO2 price can add up to 3 cents per liter of fuel, says Laberer. Typically, however, the increase does not happen abruptly but extends over several days around the turn of the year.
"When the heating season ends, diesel prices could fall significantly again," says Laberer. "Beyond that, however, there isn't much room for further decline, because if oil prices fall even further, fracking would often no longer be profitable." If this method of oil extraction fails, supply decreases, which would drive prices up again. However, there are no short-term reasons for a significant increase either. Demand is simply too low given the weakness of the global economy. "The most likely scenario is a sideways movement - meaning relatively stable fuel prices."

column3: Global Oil Prices Face Prolonged Pressure as Supply Outpaces Weak Demand
column4: Global crude prices remain under pressure as production growth is expected to outpace relatively weak demand through 2026. Forecasts from the IEA, EIA, Barclays and other analysts point to a surplus ranging from roughly 1.9 million to 4 million barrels per day, while OPEC presents a more balanced outlook. Rising output from OPEC+, the Americas and other producers, together with weaker consumption signals from China and sluggish global industrial activity, has pushed Brent toward the low-$60s and WTI below $60, with some forecasts allowing for mid-$50 prices. Contango in the Brent curve, rising tanker inventories and crude accumulating in storage indicate that supply is exceeding near-term demand. Geopolitical disruptions and low inventories may provide temporary support, but ample alternative supply has limited their price impact. Prolonged weakness could prompt producers to cut output, defer investment and reduce capacity, helping the market rebalance from 2027 onward, while OPEC+ retains the ability to respond if conditions deteriorate.

Brent crude futures settled down US$1.64 a barrel, off roughly 2.71 per cent, to US$58.92 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at US$55.27, down US$1.55, or 2.73 per cent.
"Brent has dropped this morning to below US$60 per barrel for the first time in months, as the market assesses a potential peace deal resulting in additional Russian volumes becoming available and oversupplying the market further," said Rystad analyst Janiv Shah.
The US offered to provide Nato-style security guarantees for Kyiv and European negotiators reported progress in talks on Monday, sparking optimism that an end to the war was closer. column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.
column6: Texas Leads The Charge As America Sets New Oil And Natural Gas Records
column7:
Ten counties in the U.S., in Texas and New Mexico, account for 93% of domestic oil production in the last four years analyzed by the EIA, The Center Square reported.
They are located in the Permian Basin in southeastern New Mexico and far west Texas, which produces roughly half of the crude oil and one fifth of natural gas in the country. The basin spans more than 86,000 square miles - roughly 10 times the size of New Jersey.
In the third quarter, TXOGA forecasted that "global oil demand was on track to set new records." The fourth quarter "strengthened that outlook."
"The EIA raised demand estimates twice this quarter, including a significant 500,000 b/d upward revision to 2024, and now expects demand to increase by nearly 1 million b/d per year through 2026," R. Dean Foreman, Ph.D., chief economist at TXOGA, said. "This supports a central point we have made all year: a record-sized global economy requires record volumes of oil across freight, aviation, petrochemicals, and industrial use. Supply remains the key swing variable."
In November, the EIA increased its global oil demand estimates, still expecting a record but at higher levels, also with a higher supply from the U.S. and other non-OPEC producers.
Foreman notes that EIA's baseline assumes an increase of 2.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in global supply in 2025 and an increase of 1.3 million b/d in 2026, "driven mostly by long-lead non-OPEC projects."
The EIA also assumes U.S. supply growth will slow to .2 million b/d in 2026, he notes, "repeating a pattern of conservative projections."
Foreman doesn't agree, adding, "the data suggests otherwise."
Permian Basin rig productivity in October was up by 14.1% year over year; Eagle Ford rig productivity was up 8.7% year over year.
Texas' combined crude oil and natural gas production increased by 5.8% year-to-date through November despite operating with 20.4% fewer rigs year-to-date, the perspective states.

column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

- **Venezuelan export disruption added a geopolitical premium:** U.S. tanker seizures and the blockade of sanctioned vessels disrupted China-bound shipments, while cyberattacks and tanker reluctance further impaired PDVSA logistics. Brent and WTI rebounded roughly **1.2%–1.3%**, but ample alternative supply limited the rally; prolonged storage congestion could force Venezuelan production shut-ins.

- **Russia-Ukraine developments pressured prices:** Hopes for a ceasefire and eventual sanctions relief raised the prospect of more Russian barrels returning to market, helping push **Brent below $60 and WTI below $55**. However, Ukrainian attacks, sanctions and shipping disruptions continue to threaten Russian exports and could quickly restore a risk premium.

- **U.S. crude draws offered only temporary support:** EIA inventories fell by roughly **1.3–1.8 million barrels**, with larger API draw estimates, supported by refinery demand, exports and lower imports. Nevertheless, rising gasoline and distillate stocks, weaker refining margins and expectations for renewed crude builds indicate soft underlying demand.

- **Fuel oversupply is reducing refinery appetite for crude:** U.S. gasoline inventories rose sharply and demand weakened year over year despite high refinery utilization. The resulting margin pressure, including a six-month-low crude crack spread, reinforces the broader bearish supply-demand outlook.

column3: Canada Eyes New West Coast Bitumen Pipeline to Break 90% U.S. Oil Dependence
column4: Canada is pursuing greater crude-export diversification as more than 90% of its oil currently goes to the United States. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s federal government and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith support examining a new bitumen pipeline to the West Coast, while public opinion favors expanding existing infrastructure first. Such a route would complement the Trans Mountain expansion, reduce transportation bottlenecks, improve access for Western Canadian heavy crude and bitumen, and connect oil-sands producers more directly with Asian buyers. China is the leading non-U.S. purchaser of Canadian crude shipped through Trans Mountain, while India is a major buyer of Canadian oil re-exported from U.S. Gulf Coast terminals; rising Asia-Pacific demand—from 35 million barrels per day in 2024 to a projected 41 million in 2050—strengthens the commercial case. Expanding oil-sands output from producers including Canadian Natural and Imperial Oil, alongside rising propane-plus and condensate production in Alberta and northeastern British Columbia, will increase demand for pipeline capacity and could widen regional price differentials if new infrastructure is delayed. The initiative reflects trade tensions and tariff-related pressure to reduce U.S. dependence, but faces environmental, emissions, Indigenous-rights, regulatory, and British Columbia taxation challenges. Overall, Pacific export capacity could strengthen Canada’s long-duration, non-OPEC crude supply position while increasing exposure to Asian markets and policy debates over decarbonization.
column6: Alberta's huge oil sands reserves dwarf U.S. shale
column7:
The long-term picture looks different south of the border.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects that American production will peak before 2030 and enter a long period of decline.
Having a lasting stable source of supply is important as world oil demand is expected to remain strong for decades to come.
This is particularly true in Asia, the target market for oil exports off Canada's West Coast.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects oil demand in the Asia-Pacific region will from 35 million barrels per day in 2024 to 41 million barrels per day in 2050.
The growing appeal of Alberta oil in Asian markets shows up not only in expanded Trans Mountain shipments, but also in Canadian crude being "re-exported" from U.S. Gulf Coast terminals.
According to RBN Energy, Asian buyers - primarily in China - are now the main non-U.S. buyers from Trans Mountain, while India dominates purchases of re-exports from the U.S. Gulf Coast.
BMO said the oil sands offers advantages both in steady supply and lower overall environmental impacts.
"Not only is the resulting stability ideally suited to backfill anticipated declines in world oil supply, but the long-term physical footprint may also be meaningfully lower given large-scale concentrated emissions, high water recycling rates and low well declines," BMO analysts said.
This article was originally produced by the Canadian Energy Centre.
Oil sands could maintain current production rates for more than 140 years
Pipelines at a thermal in situ oil sands facility. Photo courtesy Alberta Energy Regulator
Investor interest in Canadian oil producers, primarily in the Alberta oil sands, has picked up, and not only because of expanded export capacity from the Trans Mountain pipeline.
Enverus Intelligence Research says the real draw - and a major factor behind oil sands equities outperforming U.S. peers by about 40 per cent since January 2024 - is the resource Trans Mountain helps unlock.
Alberta's oil sands contain 167 billion barrels of reserves, nearly four times the volume in the United States.
Today's oil sands operators hold more than twice the available high-quality resources compared to U.S. shale producers, Enverus reports.
"It's a huge number - 167 billion barrels - when Alberta only produces about three million barrels a day right now," said Mike Verney, executive vice-president at McDaniel & Associates, which earlier this year updated the province's oil and gas reserves on behalf of the Alberta Energy Regulator.
Already fourth in the world, the assessment found Alberta's oil reserves increased by seven billion barrels.
Verney said the rise in reserves despite record production is in part a result of improved processes and technology.
"Oil sands companies can produce for decades at the same economic threshold as they do today. That's a great place to be," said Michael Berger, a senior analyst with Enverus.
BMO Capital Markets estimates that Alberta's oil sands reserves could maintain current production rates for more than 140 years.

column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column7:
Ten counties in the U.S., in Texas and New Mexico, account for 93% of domestic oil production in the last four years analyzed by the EIA, The Center Square reported.
They are located in the Permian Basin in southeastern New Mexico and far west Texas, which produces roughly half of the crude oil and one fifth of natural gas in the country. The basin spans more than 86,000 square miles - roughly 10 times the size of New Jersey.
In the third quarter, TXOGA forecasted that "global oil demand was on track to set new records." The fourth quarter "strengthened that outlook."
"The EIA raised demand estimates twice this quarter, including a significant 500,000 b/d upward revision to 2024, and now expects demand to increase by nearly 1 million b/d per year through 2026," R. Dean Foreman, Ph.D., chief economist at TXOGA, said. "This supports a central point we have made all year: a record-sized global economy requires record volumes of oil across freight, aviation, petrochemicals, and industrial use. Supply remains the key swing variable."
In November, the EIA increased its global oil demand estimates, still expecting a record but at higher levels, also with a higher supply from the U.S. and other non-OPEC producers.
Foreman notes that EIA's baseline assumes an increase of 2.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in global supply in 2025 and an increase of 1.3 million b/d in 2026, "driven mostly by long-lead non-OPEC projects."
The EIA also assumes U.S. supply growth will slow to .2 million b/d in 2026, he notes, "repeating a pattern of conservative projections."
Foreman doesn't agree, adding, "the data suggests otherwise."
Permian Basin rig productivity in October was up by 14.1% year over year; Eagle Ford rig productivity was up 8.7% year over year.
Texas' combined crude oil and natural gas production increased by 5.8% year-to-date through November despite operating with 20.4% fewer rigs year-to-date, the perspective states.

At the same time, oil inventories are building rapidly. Data from the International Energy Agency shows global crude stocks climbed to a four-year high in October, including oil held on tankers or in transit. Prices are now down more than 20 per cent this year, reflecting expectations of a widening surplus. The agency has warned that next year's excess supply could be the largest on record, even after OPEC+ delayed planned output increases into early 2026.
Bearish signals are also emerging across physical and futures markets. Middle Eastern crude has slipped into contango, where near-term prices trade below later deliveries, while similar patterns have appeared in parts of the US market. Margins for refined fuels such as petrol and diesel have weakened, further pressuring crude prices.
Demand-side concerns have added to the decline. Recent economic data from China pointed to slowing momentum, raising questions about fuel consumption in the world's second-largest oil consumer. In the United States, softer job growth has also signalled potential weakness in energy demand.
While falling oil prices have helped ease inflation pressures and pushed US petrol prices to their lowest levels since 2021, the slide poses growing challenges for oil-producing nations reliant on higher crude revenues.

At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

09:04 AM EST, 12/17/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Oil futures gained 2% on Wednesday, after President Donald Trump ordered a "total and complete blockade" of all oil tankers under sanctions going in and out of Venezuela, igniting fresh supply concerns.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude contract gained 1.8% at $56.26 a barrel, while Brent futures climbed 1.7% to $59.94/bbl.
Prices had dropped below $60 for the first time since 2021 on Tuesday amid optimism surrounding a potential Ukraine peace deal.
The rally was triggered by President Donald Trump's order for a naval blockade to intercept all oil tankers under sanctions from moving oil in or out of Venezuela, a move that analysts warn could abruptly halt nearly 600,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan exports primarily destined for China.
"Oil rebounded from its lowest level since 2021 after President Donald Trump ordered a blockade of sanctioned tankers to and from Venezuela," Saxo bank analysts said, adding that "the combination of low prices, robust demand and high depletion rates is likely in the coming months to sow the seeds for a stronger rebound, as sustained low prices force higher-cost producers to curb output."
Supporting prices data from the American Petroleum Institute showed that US crude oil inventories fell by 9.3 million barrels in the week ended Dec. 12.
The oil market now awaits crude inventory data from the US Energy Information Administration for clues on supply-demand balance.

column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.

The Ukraine-Russia Peace Path
The most significant downward pressure on oil prices this month stems from renewed optimism regarding the conflict in Ukraine. Negotiations in Berlin suggest that consensus has been reached on approximately 90 per cent of the plan.
Market Impact: Investors have begun pricing out the "geopolitical risk premium." A formal ceasefire would likely lead to the lifting of sanctions on Russian energy firms, potentially releasing up to 170 million barrels of oil currently stored on water back into the global market.
Russian Crude Exports: November and YTD Performance
Russia's energy sector faced a challenging November as Western sanctions and tighter enforcement weighed on logistics and buyer sentiment. November Exports: Russian crude exports fell by approximately 420,000 barrels per day (kb/d) in November, bringing total oil exports down to 6.9 million barrels per day (mb/d). the annual  exports has remained surprisingly resilient. Total supply is up by roughly 120 kb/d compared to 2024 levels, though growth has been significantly stymied by the late-year sanctions on major producers like Rosneft and Lukoil.
Global Demand & Supply Projections (OPEC, IEA, EIA)
The three major energy agencies released their final 2025 reports this week, revealing a consensus on a looming supply surplus but differing on the scale of demand growth.
OPEC shows the most affirmative forecast with 1.3mbpd jump in demand and expect resilient physical markets despite price drops.
IEA forecast demand at 830,000 mbpd but supply will outcast demand by 3.8 mbpd by end of 2026. The IEA warns that while global inventories are at four-year highs, the surplus is currently "masked" by regional tightness in refined products, caused by unplanned refinery outages and upcoming EU bans on Russian-derived fuels.
EIA is seeing demand at 1.1 million | 104.5 mb/d and cautiously optimistic, citing petrochemicals as a driver.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

09:04 AM EST, 12/17/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Oil futures gained 2% on Wednesday, after President Donald Trump ordered a "total and complete blockade" of all oil tankers under sanctions going in and out of Venezuela, igniting fresh supply concerns.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude contract gained 1.8% at $56.26 a barrel, while Brent futures climbed 1.7% to $59.94/bbl.
Prices had dropped below $60 for the first time since 2021 on Tuesday amid optimism surrounding a potential Ukraine peace deal.
The rally was triggered by President Donald Trump's order for a naval blockade to intercept all oil tankers under sanctions from moving oil in or out of Venezuela, a move that analysts warn could abruptly halt nearly 600,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan exports primarily destined for China.
"Oil rebounded from its lowest level since 2021 after President Donald Trump ordered a blockade of sanctioned tankers to and from Venezuela," Saxo bank analysts said, adding that "the combination of low prices, robust demand and high depletion rates is likely in the coming months to sow the seeds for a stronger rebound, as sustained low prices force higher-cost producers to curb output."
Supporting prices data from the American Petroleum Institute showed that US crude oil inventories fell by 9.3 million barrels in the week ended Dec. 12.
The oil market now awaits crude inventory data from the US Energy Information Administration for clues on supply-demand balance.

column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.

Data from the International Energy Agency shows global crude stocks climbed to a four-year high in October, including oil held on tankers or in transit. The agency has warned that next year's excess supply could be the largest on record, even after OPEC+ delayed planned output increases into early 2026.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. column3: Canada Eyes New West Coast Bitumen Pipeline to Break 90% U.S. Oil Dependence
column4: Canada is pursuing greater crude-export diversification as more than 90% of its oil currently goes to the United States. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s federal government and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith support examining a new bitumen pipeline to the West Coast, while public opinion favors expanding existing infrastructure first. Such a route would complement the Trans Mountain expansion, reduce transportation bottlenecks, improve access for Western Canadian heavy crude and bitumen, and connect oil-sands producers more directly with Asian buyers. China is the leading non-U.S. purchaser of Canadian crude shipped through Trans Mountain, while India is a major buyer of Canadian oil re-exported from U.S. Gulf Coast terminals; rising Asia-Pacific demand—from 35 million barrels per day in 2024 to a projected 41 million in 2050—strengthens the commercial case. Expanding oil-sands output from producers including Canadian Natural and Imperial Oil, alongside rising propane-plus and condensate production in Alberta and northeastern British Columbia, will increase demand for pipeline capacity and could widen regional price differentials if new infrastructure is delayed. The initiative reflects trade tensions and tariff-related pressure to reduce U.S. dependence, but faces environmental, emissions, Indigenous-rights, regulatory, and British Columbia taxation challenges. Overall, Pacific export capacity could strengthen Canada’s long-duration, non-OPEC crude supply position while increasing exposure to Asian markets and policy debates over decarbonization.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column3: Ukrainian Strikes and Western Sanctions Squeeze Russian Oil Exports
column4: Russian crude exports are facing simultaneous disruption from Ukrainian attacks, infrastructure outages and tightening Western sanctions. Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have hit at least 28 Russian refineries, including the Slavyansky refinery and the Nikolaevskaya depot, worsening domestic fuel shortages and reducing refining and export capacity; a separate attack forced the closure of a Baltic Sea oil terminal, while maritime-drone risks have pushed tankers leaving Novorossiysk onto longer routes through waters near Georgia and Turkey. Damage to a Caspian Pipeline Consortium mooring also temporarily disrupted a system carrying about 1.6 million barrels per day of Kazakhstan’s crude. U.S., EU and UK sanctions on Russian producers, infrastructure, tankers, traders and the shadow fleet—including new EU designations covering nearly 600 vessels—are increasing legal, logistical and shipping constraints, with Washington considering further measures if Moscow rejects a Ukraine peace proposal. Sanctions and scrutiny have sharply reduced Indian purchases of Urals crude, from roughly 2 million barrels per day in June to an expected 800,000 barrels per day in December, leaving cargoes and tankers idling near China and pushing Urals discounts wider. Russian oil-product shipments fell to about 1.7 million barrels per day in the first half of November, a more than three-year low. Although alternative routes, opaque shipping practices and rerouting may preserve some flows, floating storage, longer voyages and accumulating unsold cargoes are raising costs and uncertainty. These risks support crude prices by threatening seaborne supply, though the broader global oil surplus limits the overall price impact.

column3: U.S. Crude Stock Draws Lift WTI and Brent, but Surplus Concerns Persist
column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

column7:

column6: US Oil Update: Crude Up Almost 3% After Trump Orders Venezuela Oil Tanker Blockade
column7:
05:12 PM EST, 12/17/2025 (MT Newswires) -- Crude oil futures rallied in after-hours trading on Wednesday, supported by President Trump's order to impose a complete blockade of all sanctioned oil tankers entering and leaving Venezuela, as the US reportedly weighs new Russian sanctions to spur a peace deal.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude jumped 2.95% to $56.90 per barrel, while Brent futures were up 2.85% to $60.60/bbl.
A bullish inventory report added upward pressure to the benchmarks. US crude stockpiles fell by 1.3 million barrels to 424.4 million bbls in the week ended Dec.12, the Energy Information Administration said in its weekly report on Wednesday. The American Petroleum Institute also reported a decrease in US crude oil inventories of 9.3 million bbls in the week ended Dec. 12, following a 4.8-million-barrel draw the previous week.
Trump ordered a "total and complete" blockade of sanctioned oil tankers leaving and entering Venezuela on Tuesday. The move follows the US's seizure of a sanctioned oil tanker off Venezuela's coast last week.
Venezuela exported about 600,000 b/d of oil in November, ING strategists said in a Wednesday note, adding that these volumes are likely to fall given the latest developments.
Meanwhile, the US is reportedly considering new sanctions against Russia's energy sector to tighten pressure on Moscow should President Vladimir Putin reject a peace deal with Ukraine. The new measures could include targeting Russia's shadow fleet of oil tankers and traders who facilitate crude exports, according to media reports.
Additionally, the US Department of the Treasury said Wednesday it had sanctioned a Mexican cartel allegedly running a vast fuel-theft operation that authorities say has distorted energy markets and siphoned billions of dollars from Mexico's state oil firm.
Mexican cartels steal billions of dollars from Pemex, fuel rampant violence and corruption across Mexico, and undercut legitimate oil and natural gas companies in the US, the Treasury Department said in a statement.
Gains were capped by projections of a supply glut, with supply forecast to exceed demand in Q4 and next year, driven by rising production from within the OPEC+ group and several non-OPEC countries in the Americas.

column3: U.S. Crude Stock Draws Lift WTI and Brent, but Surplus Concerns Persist
column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column4: U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.

column4: A ransomware-related cyberattack on Venezuela’s state oil company PDVSA disrupted centralized administrative systems and prompted the temporary isolation of oilfields, refineries, ports, and other facilities. Workers shifted to manual delivery records, allowing terminal operations and navigation to resume, but exports remained heavily constrained. Tankers were reportedly reluctant to leave Venezuelan waters following the U.S. seizure of the Skipper and announcement of a blockade, while Venezuelan crude exports had already fallen sharply from more than 900,000 barrels per day in November. Chevron continued loading cargoes for the United States, but the combination of cyber risks, manual procedures, immobilized tankers, and potential U.S. interdiction threatens Venezuela’s production logistics and near-term global crude supply.
column6: Trump's Tanker Blockade Threat Paralyzes Venezuelan Oil Exports
column7:
Dec 17 (Reuters) - Venezuela's state-run oil company PDVSA resumed loading crude and fuel cargoes on Wednesday after suspending operations at terminals on Sunday due to a cyberattack, although most exports remain on hold as the U.S. threatens to enforce a blockade on tankers under sanctions, according to three company sources, traders and shipping data.
Venezuela's crude exports have fallen sharply from the more than 900,000 barrels per day it shipped in November since the U.S. seized a sanctioned vessel a week ago. Operators have kept loaded ships in Venezuelan waters for fear they would be seized if they set sail for China, the destination for most of Venezuela's oil.
Even as ships resume loading at PDVSA's terminals, it is unclear how many would sail into international waters. U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a blockade of all oil tankers under sanctions sailing into or out of Venezuelan waters.

column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. The result is volatile, two-sided trading as markets weigh potential sanctions relief and normalized Russian flows against continuing disruptions and current sanctions that have reduced exports.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.

column3: Permian Efficiency Keeps U.S. Shale Output High Despite 20% Rig Slump
column4: U.S. shale output remains elevated despite a sharp decline in drilling activity, demonstrating gains in well productivity and drilling efficiency. The Permian Basin, which supplies about half of U.S. crude and is projected to produce a record 6.76 million barrels per day in December, is the main source of this resilience. Permian rig productivity rose 14.1% year over year, while Texas oil and gas output increased 5.8% year to date despite a 20.4% fall in the rig count; nationally, production near 13.8 million barrels per day has been sustained with only about 414 active oil rigs, near a four-year low. Longer laterals—58% longer on average in the Midland Basin than in 2015—together with improved drilling software, multi-well fracturing, electric fracking, better infrastructure and consolidation are enabling operators to recover more hydrocarbons per well. ExxonMobil and Chevron are using these technologies to extend the Permian’s productive life, while Occidental continues to invest in basin infrastructure. Low breakeven costs of roughly $30-$40 per barrel allow producers to maintain output even with WTI below $60, although mature acreage, rising steel, labor and compliance costs, weak oilfield activity and cautious capital spending point to slower growth or a plateau. With U.S. production expected to remain around 13.5 million barrels per day through 2026, shale efficiency and high base output are sustaining global supply and limiting upward pressure on crude prices.

Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude jumped 2.95% to $56.90 per barrel, while Brent futures were up 2.85% to $60.60/bbl.
A bullish inventory report added upward pressure to the benchmarks. US crude stockpiles fell by 1.3 million barrels to 424.4 million bbls in the week ended Dec.12, the Energy Information Administration said in its weekly report on Wednesday. Trump ordered a "total and complete" blockade of sanctioned oil tankers leaving and entering Venezuela on Tuesday. The move follows the US's seizure of a sanctioned oil tanker off Venezuela's coast last week.
Venezuela exported about 600,000 b/d of oil in November, ING strategists said in a Wednesday note, adding that these volumes are likely to fall given the latest developments.

The new measures could include targeting Russia's shadow fleet of oil tankers and traders who facilitate crude exports, according to media reports.
Additionally, the US Department of the Treasury said Wednesday it had sanctioned a Mexican cartel allegedly running a vast fuel-theft operation that authorities say has distorted energy markets and siphoned billions of dollars from Mexico's state oil firm.
Mexican cartels steal billions of dollars from Pemex, fuel rampant violence and corruption across Mexico, and undercut legitimate oil and natural gas companies in the US, the Treasury Department said in a statement.

column3: OPEC+ Output Revival and Surging Non-OPEC Supply Push Oil Toward a 4 Million-Barrel-a-Day Glut
column4: Global crude markets are moving toward a substantial surplus as OPEC+ unwinds earlier production cuts while non-OPEC output remains strong. OPEC+ has restored roughly 2.9 million barrels per day since April 2025 and plans further increases, including about 137,000 barrels per day in December, although additional hikes are scheduled to pause in the first quarter of 2026; its existing agreement still implies potential growth of around 1.3 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026. At the same time, U.S. production is near record levels above 13.8 million barrels per day, while Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada, Norway, the Gulf of Mexico and other new projects are adding barrels, condensate, oil-sands supply and U.S. natural gas liquids. Global supply reached about 107.5 million barrels per day in November despite temporary declines in Russia, Venezuela and Brazil, with year-on-year growth near 4 million barrels per day. Forecasts point to supply growth substantially exceeding demand in 2026: the IEA estimates a surplus of roughly 3.8–4.0 million barrels per day, while other analysts project supply growth of 2.1–3.2 million barrels per day against demand growth of only about 0.8 million. Rising inventories, increased crude held on water, contango, weaker refining margins and reduced refinery buying reflect the imbalance. The surplus has pressured Brent and WTI to their lowest levels since early 2021 and could drive Brent into the $50s or lower if OPEC+ does not impose additional restraint or demand strengthens. Longer term, executives including ExxonMobil’s Prasanna V. Joshi and TotalEnergies’ Patrick Pouyanné warn that OPEC+ will need to manage the glut, even as sustained demand may eventually require renewed upstream investment.

column3: Ukrainian Strikes and Western Sanctions Squeeze Russian Oil Exports
column4: Russian crude exports are facing simultaneous disruption from Ukrainian attacks, infrastructure outages and tightening Western sanctions. Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have hit at least 28 Russian refineries, including the Slavyansky refinery and the Nikolaevskaya depot, worsening domestic fuel shortages and reducing refining and export capacity; a separate attack forced the closure of a Baltic Sea oil terminal, while maritime-drone risks have pushed tankers leaving Novorossiysk onto longer routes through waters near Georgia and Turkey. Damage to a Caspian Pipeline Consortium mooring also temporarily disrupted a system carrying about 1.6 million barrels per day of Kazakhstan’s crude. U.S., EU and UK sanctions on Russian producers, infrastructure, tankers, traders and the shadow fleet—including new EU designations covering nearly 600 vessels—are increasing legal, logistical and shipping constraints, with Washington considering further measures if Moscow rejects a Ukraine peace proposal. Sanctions and scrutiny have sharply reduced Indian purchases of Urals crude, from roughly 2 million barrels per day in June to an expected 800,000 barrels per day in December, leaving cargoes and tankers idling near China and pushing Urals discounts wider. Russian oil-product shipments fell to about 1.7 million barrels per day in the first half of November, a more than three-year low. Although alternative routes, opaque shipping practices and rerouting may preserve some flows, floating storage, longer voyages and accumulating unsold cargoes are raising costs and uncertainty. These risks support crude prices by threatening seaborne supply, though the broader global oil surplus limits the overall price impact.

A fleet of tankers loaded with Russia's Urals crude has gathered off China's eastern coast after India-the largest buyer of the grade-curbed purchases due to Western sanctions.
Bloomberg reported this, citing data from Kpler, according to Ukrinform.
As of Wednesday, at least five vessels carrying about 3.4 million barrels of oil were idling in the Yellow Sea. The ships are located near Shandong province, a hub for independent refineries.
The buildup of Urals crude off China is a unique situation that has drawn the attention of oil traders worldwide, as Chinese refineries are not typical buyers of this grade, which is loaded at distant western Russian ports. They usually prefer Russian crude from eastern terminals due to proximity and higher diesel quality. However, tighter US oversight of Russian oil shipments to India, along with sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil, have forced Urals sellers to seek alternative buyers in East Asia. According to local officials, India's imports are expected to total about 800,000 barrels per day in December, down from a peak of 2 million barrels per day in June.

column3: Russia-Ukraine Peace Hopes Send Oil Below $60 as Traders Price In Sanctions Relief
column4: Progress in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations is reducing crude’s geopolitical risk premium as traders anticipate a ceasefire could end attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, improve production and logistics, and eventually ease U.S. and European sanctions. Reports of U.S. and European diplomatic efforts, possible security guarantees for Kyiv, and discussions involving President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky have raised expectations that more Russian barrels could return to established international markets, potentially releasing oil held in storage or on water. This is particularly bearish in an already well-supplied market, contributing to Brent falling below $60 and WTI below $55, with some scenarios pointing toward prices in the low-$50s. However, the outlook remains uncertain: unresolved territorial issues, Russia’s reluctance to concede, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil infrastructure, shipping constraints, and the possibility of failed talks or renewed escalation could quickly restore the premium; a major escalation could instead push crude toward $90. column6: Crude Oil Prices Drop to 4-Year Low!
column7:
The global crude oil commodity market witnessed a sharp drop in prices as it hit the lowest level not seen since early 2021. The decline was driven by expectations of a worsening supply glut and positive developments in peace talks in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
During Wednesday's trading in the Asian session, Brent oil fell more than 2% to trade below $59 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell more than 3%, reaching below $55 per barrel.
Cumulatively, both energy products are expected to close the year with an annual loss of more than 20% due to a supply glut in the global market.

column6: SBM Offshore extends FPSO contracts in Angola through 2032
column7:
(WO) - Offshore contractor SBM Offshore has secured a contract extension for the lease and operation of the FPSOs Mondo and Saxi Batuque on Block 15 offshore Angola, extending its involvement in the assets through 2032.
The agreement was signed with Esso Exploration Angola (Block 15) Ltd., an affiliate of ExxonMobil and operator of the block. The extension includes life-extension activities such as equipment replacement and refurbishment to maintain safety, reliability and operational performance over the coming decade. Work under the new scope is expected to begin in 2026.
SBM Offshore said the contract reflects its long-standing capabilities in managing complex brownfield offshore projects and in the operation and maintenance of deepwater floating production systems. The FPSOs are key assets supporting ongoing production from Block 15, one of Angola's core offshore developments.
"We are very pleased with the contract extension of FPSOs Mondo and Saxi Batuque," said Øivind Tangen, CEO of SBM Offshore. "This allows us to maintain our structure and scale in Angola and, most importantly, provide job security to our teams. We remain committed to safe and reliable operations throughout the extension period."
Block 15 is operated by Esso Exploration Angola (Block 15) Ltd., with partners including Azule Angola, Equinor Angola Block 15 A.S. and Sonangol E&P. SBM Offshore has operated in Angola for more than three decades and said the extension reinforces its long-term role in supporting the country's offshore energy sector.

column3: EU Moves Toward Full Russian Oil Ban to Crimp Kremlin Revenues
column4: The European Parliament has agreed to advance legislation for a comprehensive ban on Russian oil imports, following measures to phase out Russian LNG and pipeline gas. The European Commission is expected to propose the oil legislation in early 2026, with implementation as soon as possible and no later than late 2027. The policy aims to reduce Russia’s fossil-fuel revenues and limit its ability to use energy dependence as geopolitical leverage. If enacted, Russia would need to redirect more crude to Asian and other markets, likely increasing shipping distances, sanctions exposure, discounts and logistical complexity, while forcing the EU to secure alternative suppliers.
column6: EU draws the line on Russian gas with gradual ban from 2026, oil set to follow suit in 2027
column7:
As a result of this legislation move, spot-market Russian LNG will be banned from the EU once the regulation enters into force in early 2026, while pipeline gas imports will be phased out by September 30, 2027. During negotiations, the co-legislators advanced the phase-out timelines for most import contracts. The new law establishes penalties to be enforced by member states against operators for infringements.
During negotiations with the Danish presidency of the Council, MEPs also pushed for the banning of all imports of Russian oil and secured a commitment by the European Commission to present legislation for this in early 2026, so an effective ban can be enforced as soon as possible and no later than late-2027.
Ville Niinistö (Greens/EFA, Finland), MEP for the Industry, Research and Energy Committee (ITRE), commented: "This is historic: the EU is taking a giant step towards a new era free of Russian gas and oil. Russia can never again use fossil fuel exports as a weapon against Europe. Our key priorities were to accelerate the timeline for banning pipeline gas as much as possible, prohibit long-term LNG contracts one year earlier than foreseen, and prevent circumvention of these new rules.
"Now, we must act without delay to implement this agreement and turn our attention to oil imports, where we will hold the European Commission to its commitment to make a proposal early in 2026."
In addition, the MEPs pushed for stricter conditions under which a temporary suspension of the import ban can occur in emergency situations in relation to EU energy security. Operators will have to provide customs authorities with stricter and more detailed evidence of the country of production of their gas before its import or storage to close loopholes and mitigate the risk that the rules are being circumvented.
Given its determination to shake off the shackles of dependence on Russian oil and gas imports, the European Union (EU) has decided to lay down the law on these fossil fuels by holding the line on the proposed gradual ban on imports of pipeline gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) from next year, with oil expected to suffer the same fate in 2027 in response to what is being portrayed as Russia's systematic weaponisation of energy supplies.

column3: U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts
column4: U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

column3: DNO Secures Up to $410 Million in Liquidity Through ExxonMobil and Shell Oil Deals
column4: From January 1, 2026, Norwegian operator DNO will sell its North Sea oil production roughly equally to ExxonMobil Asia Pacific and Shell Trading and Shipping. ExxonMobil’s two-year offtake agreement is supported by a revolving credit facility of up to $185 million, while Shell’s initial one-year agreement includes a $225 million prepayment facility arranged with a European bank. Together, the deals provide up to $410 million in production-linked financing, strengthening DNO’s liquidity without requiring an asset sale. Combined with DNO’s existing gas agreement with ENGIE, such financing could reach $910 million, giving ExxonMobil and Shell secure access to North Sea crude while helping DNO fund operations and future development amid volatile oil prices.
column6: DNO secures North Sea oil offtake agreements with ExxonMobil and Shell
column7:
Norwegian independent DNO ASA has finalized new North Sea oil offtake agreements with subsidiaries of ExxonMobil and Shell, effective Jan. 1, 2026, securing up to $410 million in related financing facilities.
Under the agreements, ExxonMobil Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. will lift approximately half of DNO's North Sea oil production under a two-year offtake arrangement supported by a revolving credit facility of up to $185 million. The remaining production will be marketed by Shell Trading and Shipping Company Limited under an initial one-year offtake agreement, backed by a prepayment facility of up to $225 million arranged with a European bank.
DNO said the financing terms associated with the offtake agreements are competitive and provide additional financial flexibility amid volatile market conditions. The company noted that the facilities will support continued operational and growth initiatives across its North Sea portfolio.
The new oil offtake arrangements build on DNO's existing gas offtake and financing agreement with ENGIE SA, announced earlier this year. Together, the oil and gas agreements provide DNO with access to up to $910 million in production-linked financing tied to its North Sea assets.
DNO operates a growing portfolio on the Norwegian Continental Shelf and has emphasized the role of long-term offtake partnerships in strengthening balance sheet resilience and funding future development.
